subject: chemistry
question_text: Using ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, explain how the signs of ΔH and ΔS and the temperature decide whether a process is spontaneous.

verification.note: PREDICTED, not asked. This question comes from the enumeration sweep of the Thermodynamics syllabus: the book asks Gibbs energy only as a two-mark definition (VSAQ 8), and the four ΔH/ΔS sign combinations — the standard examination table for spontaneity — appear nowhere in the chapter. steps.label: Equation and criterion
steps.why: ΔG collects the enthalpy change and the entropy change into one signed number; its sign is the complete test for the direction of the process.
common_mistakes: Writing ΔG = ΔH + TΔS — the entropy term is subtracted.
steps.memory_tip: One equation, one test: compute ΔH − TΔS and read the sign.
steps.margin_note: Equation plus the three sign readings.

steps.label: The four sign cases
lines: ΔH < 0, ΔS < 0: spontaneous only at low T,
where the TΔS term is small.
ΔH > 0, ΔS > 0: spontaneous only at high T,
where TΔS is larger than ΔH.
steps.why: T is always positive (kelvin), so the sign of ΔG follows from how large TΔS is compared with ΔH — the temperature decides the two mixed cases.
common_mistakes: Forgetting that T is in kelvin and always positive.
Calling an endothermic process never spontaneous — with ΔS > 0 it becomes spontaneous at high temperature.
steps.memory_tip: Two clean cases (always, never) and two temperature-decided cases (low T, high T).
steps.margin_note: Both marks are here: all four combinations, each with its condition.

steps.label: Example
lines: Example: melting of ice has ΔH > 0 and
ΔS > 0, so it is spontaneous above 273 K
steps.why: Ice melting is the everyday case of the fourth row: an endothermic change that the entropy term makes spontaneous once the temperature is high enough.
common_mistakes: Choosing an example whose signs do not match the case being illustrated.
steps.memory_tip: Ice melts above 0 °C and not below — one fact that fixes the whole fourth case.
steps.margin_note: Any correctly signed example is accepted; ice is the simplest.
